title: Ehrlichia spp. and Ehrlichioses: Diversity, Distribution, Zoonotic Potential, and Challenges for Surveillance from a One Health Perspective
content: Tick-borne diseases represent a challenge to both human and animal health, but the strength of the available evidence varies among Ehrlichia species. This critical narrative review analyzed the diversity, geographic distribution, vectors, hosts, zoonotic potential, diagnosis, and surveillance of ehrlichioses. The synthesis distinguished among seroreactivity, molecular detection, isolation, clinical association, vector competence, and reservoir competence. Ehrlichia chaffeensis, E. ewingii, and E. muris subsp. eauclairensis are established human pathogens. Ehrlichia canis causes a widely distributed veterinary disease and has been molecularly confirmed in human infections; however, its frequency and population-level relevance remain uncertain. For E. minasensis, E. japonica, and provisional taxa, detection in animals or ticks alone is insufficient to demonstrate zoonotic transmission. In Latin America, particularly in Brazil, evidence of human infection remains limited, is often based on serology, and contrasts with negative molecular investigations. The absence of a specific nationwide mandatory notification system, low clinical suspicion, and limited access to PCR contribute to underdiagnosis and underreporting. Integrated surveillance is therefore recommended, based on the early collection of human samples, investigation of animals and ticks linked to exposure, molecular characterization, and joint spatial and environmental analysis.
